body.heading: An ancient pocket game
paragraphs: Children in ancient Egypt and Rome played with marbles of stone, clay and nuts; the game has been reinvented in every century since, in glass, steel and plastic. Its genius is portability: a whole stadium fits in a pocket, and the pitch is a chalk circle on any flat ground.

The classic game is Ringers. Draw a ring about three metres across (smaller for young players). Place thirteen target marbles in the centre, often in a cross. Players shoot from the ring's edge, trying to knock targets out of the circle while keeping their own shooter inside play.

body.heading: Knuckle down: the shot
paragraphs: The classic shot gave us the phrase “knuckle down”. Rest your knuckle on the ground, curl your shooter marble in your index finger, and flick it with your thumb. A marble that leaves the ring counts; a shooter that flies out of the circle may cost you your turn — agree the local law before you begin.

Before the game, agree the most important rule of all: are you playing “for fair” (everyone keeps their own marbles) or “for keeps” (won marbles change owners)? Generations of playground diplomacy have turned on that single sentence.

body.heading: Try it: set up a family ring
paragraphs: No marbles? Buttons, bottle caps and smooth pebbles all substitute bravely. Mark targets in the centre, shoot in turns, and keep score by marbles knocked out rather than marbles owned — the friendliest scoring of all.

Add a championship touch: name your shooter, keep a season table on the fridge, and let the youngest player choose the ring size. Marbles rewards touch more than strength, which is why grandparents are so often its champions.

takeaway: Marbles is the original pocket game: a chalk circle, a steady knuckle, and rules your grandparents would recognise.
